Topshiriqlar: Matching headings, True/False/Not Given, boʻshliq toʻldirish va test savollari, jumladan «reference» savoli (olmosh nimaga ishora qilishini topish). Taxminan 20 daqiqa. Maslahat: olmosh soʻralganda oldingi gapni oʻqing — ishora qilingan ot odatda yaqin joyda turadi.

paragraphs.en: Why do people spend hours on activities that earn them nothing? Amateur musicians practise scales late into the evening, volunteers maintain hiking trails at weekends, and countless contributors write and correct entries in online encyclopedias without payment or public credit. Such behaviour sits uneasily with the assumption, common in both economics and everyday management, that people work chiefly in response to rewards and punishments. Psychologists have long sought to account for it by distinguishing between two broad kinds of motivation.

Intrinsic motivation refers to doing something because it is inherently interesting or satisfying: the activity is, in effect, its own reward. Extrinsic motivation, by contrast, refers to doing something in order to obtain an outcome that is separable from the activity itself, whether a salary, a grade, praise or the avoidance of a penalty. Most real activities involve a mixture of the two, and neither is automatically superior. Nevertheless, the distinction has proved valuable, not least because it draws attention to the possibility that the two forms of motivation may interact in unexpected ways.

The most provocative evidence for such interaction comes from research on what is called the overjustification effect. In a classic study conducted in the early 1970s, nursery-school children who already showed an interest in drawing were divided into groups. Some were told in advance that they would receive a certificate for drawing, others received the same reward unexpectedly, and others received nothing. When the children were later observed during free play, those who had expected and received the reward spent less time drawing than the other children did. The reward, it seemed, had transformed an enjoyable pastime into something done for a prize.

Subsequent research has shown that the picture is considerably more nuanced than the most dramatic interpretations suggest. Rewards appear most likely to undermine interest when they are expected, tangible and dependent simply on doing the task, and when the activity was enjoyable to begin with. Verbal feedback that conveys information about competence, by contrast, may sustain or even enhance interest, and rewards for tasks that people find tedious are unlikely to destroy an enthusiasm that never existed. Reviews combining the results of many studies have reached somewhat different conclusions about the size and generality of the effect, and the debate has not been entirely resolved.

Why should a reward ever reduce interest? One influential answer is offered by self-determination theory, which has been developed over several decades. According to this framework, people have three basic psychological needs: autonomy, the sense that one's actions are self-endorsed rather than imposed; competence, the experience of acting effectively; and relatedness, the feeling of being connected to and cared for by others. Rewards and other external pressures are thought to undermine intrinsic motivation chiefly when they are experienced as controlling, since they then shift the perceived reason for acting from within the person to outside.

The implications for schools and workplaces are considerable. Environments that rely heavily on surveillance, deadlines imposed without explanation and rewards made contingent on narrow targets risk producing compliance rather than engagement. Teachers and managers who offer meaningful choices, explain the reasons behind requests and acknowledge the perspectives of those they supervise are, according to this research, more likely to foster lasting motivation. This does not mean abandoning structure; rather, it means providing structure in a way that supports, instead of overriding, a person's sense of agency.

It would be misleading, however, to present extrinsic motivation as inherently harmful. Self-determination theory itself describes a continuum along which externally prompted behaviour can gradually become internalised. A student who initially revises only to pass an examination may come to value the subject for its own sake, or at least to recognise its personal importance; a nurse who follows hygiene procedures because they are required may, over time, follow them because she understands why they matter. Such internalised motivation, though not strictly intrinsic, appears to be far more durable than behaviour sustained only by external pressure.

Rewards, in short, are neither a universal solution nor an inevitable threat. Their effect depends on what they communicate: whether they are perceived as an attempt to control or as recognition of genuine achievement. Those who wish to motivate others might therefore do well to ask not only what incentives to offer, but whether the conditions they create allow people to feel capable, connected and, above all, the authors of their own actions.

questions.statement: In the classic study, children who received a reward unexpectedly drew less afterwards than children who had been promised one.

explain.uz: Matnga koʻra kamroq chizganlar aynan mukofotni oldindan kutganlar edi: «those who had expected and received the reward spent less time drawing than the other children did».

questions.statement: The certificates in the classic study were chosen by the children's parents.

explain.uz: Sertifikat haqida faqat u mukofot boʻlgani aytilgan; uni kim tanlagani haqida maʼlumot yoʻq.

questions.statement: Researchers now fully agree on how large and widespread the overjustification effect is.

explain.uz: «Reviews … have reached somewhat different conclusions about the size and generality of the effect, and the debate has not been entirely resolved».

questions.statement: According to self-determination theory, rewards are most damaging to interest when people experience them as controlling.

explain.uz: «are thought to undermine intrinsic motivation chiefly when they are experienced as controlling» — «damaging» = «undermine».

questions.prompt: Verbal feedback that gives information about ___ may help to maintain people's interest.

explain.uz: «Verbal feedback that conveys information about competence … may sustain or even enhance interest» — «maintain» = «sustain».

questions.prompt: Environments built on surveillance and narrow targets may result in ___ rather than genuine engagement.
Self-determination theory describes a ___ along which behaviour first prompted from outside can become internalised.

explain.uz: «describes a continuum along which externally prompted behaviour can gradually become internalised».
